tweets.text:
New research from Replit on scaling laws for agent swarms. 

We show that scaling the number of agents can yield dramatic performance gains, but unlike traditional scaling laws, more compute doesn't necessarily translate into better results, and how agents organize themselves matters.

- Given a fixed two-hour window, Opus 5.5 went from a 3.7x speedup on NumPy with one agent to 18.9x with 32 agents.

- GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent but exhibited negative scaling beyond 8 agents.

- Models spontaneously developed different organizational structures. Decentralized swarms scaled better than those that relied on centralized coordination.

- The parallelizability of the problem was a strong predictor of swarm performance.

- Interestingly, individual model intelligence is a poor predictor of collective intelligence.

We’re also open-sourcing Optimization-Bench to advance research into this new dimension of inference-time scaling.

https://t.co/RXBU7aM5FE
tweets.summary_zh: Replit 最近发布了一项研究，研究了多个 AI 代理（小助手）一起工作时的表现。结果发现，增加代理的数量可以大幅提高效率，但并不是所有情况下计算能力提高会带来更好的效果，代理们各自的组织方式也很重要。比如，在固定时间内，使用 32 个代理进行计算的速度提升远超过一个代理。而且，当代理之间能够自由合作时，效率更高。总的来说，单个代理的智能水平并不一定能预测整个团队的表现。Replit 还将开放一些工具来帮助大家研究这个新领域。

tweets.text:
This is a pretty key insight. Services businesses are always held back by their ability to deliver outcomes to customers. 

That scaling essentially only could come from headcount, and no matter how much demand you saw, there was always a finite amount of talent you could get for the problem you were going after. Not to mention, the customer generally always wants the work done faster, at a lower price, or at a higher quality.

Agents entirely change the calculus here, because now we can scale output in a way that’s decoupled from the among of time that goes in. A single engineer can have the output of dozens of engineers before. A single designer can probably build out your entire design system and brand. And so on.

Well why isn’t this just all agents then? Because the key is to still have experts on the front end that actually can ensure the right outcomes are delivered from agents.

It’s likely that we’re going to see this in a wide variety of categories. You’ll see this in cyber security, advertising and marketing, legal, accounting, IT transformation, and a number of other historically people-only services industries.

It’s a great time if you’re starting one of these businesses, or if you have the capability to transform an existing one.
tweets.summary_zh: 服务行业一直受到提供客户结果能力的限制，通常只能通过增加员工来扩大规模，但人才是有限的。现在有了AI（智能代理），一位工程师能产生之前多位工程师的工作量，这样可以更快、更便宜、更高质量地完成任务。不过，还是需要专家来确保AI能达到预期的效果。接下来，AI将改变很多传统依靠人力的行业，比如网络安全、广告、法律和会计等，如果你想启动或转型这些业务，现在正是好时机！

tweets.text:
New research from Replit on scaling laws for agent swarms. 

We show that scaling the number of agents can yield dramatic performance gains, but unlike traditional scaling laws, more compute doesn't necessarily translate into better results, and how agents organize themselves matters.

- Given a fixed two-hour window, Opus 5.5 went from a 3.7x speedup on NumPy with one agent to 18.9x with 32 agents.

- GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent but exhibited negative scaling beyond 8 agents.

- Models spontaneously developed different organizational structures. Decentralized swarms scaled better than those that relied on centralized coordination.

- The parallelizability of the problem was a strong predictor of swarm performance.

- Interestingly, individual model intelligence is a poor predictor of collective intelligence.

We’re also open-sourcing Optimization-Bench to advance research into this new dimension of inference-time scaling.

https://t.co/RXBU7aM5FE
tweets.summary_zh: Replit的新研究发现，增加AI代理（agent）的数量可以显著提高性能，但并不是简单增加计算能力就能保证更好的结果，代理的组织方式也很重要。比如，在固定的两小时内，使用32个代理的情况下，速度提高了18.9倍，而单个代理的速度提升只有3.7倍。同时，研究还发现，模型的智能水平无法有效预测团队的整体智能表现。他们还计划开源一个名为Optimization-Bench的工具，帮助推动这一领域的进一步研究。

tweets.text:
This is a pretty key insight. Services businesses are always held back by their ability to deliver outcomes to customers. 

That scaling essentially only could come from headcount, and no matter how much demand you saw, there was always a finite amount of talent you could get for the problem you were going after. Not to mention, the customer generally always wants the work done faster, at a lower price, or at a higher quality.

Agents entirely change the calculus here, because now we can scale output in a way that’s decoupled from the among of time that goes in. A single engineer can have the output of dozens of engineers before. A single designer can probably build out your entire design system and brand. And so on.

Well why isn’t this just all agents then? Because the key is to still have experts on the front end that actually can ensure the right outcomes are delivered from agents.

It’s likely that we’re going to see this in a wide variety of categories. You’ll see this in cyber security, advertising and marketing, legal, accounting, IT transformation, and a number of other historically people-only services industries.

It’s a great time if you’re starting one of these businesses, or if you have the capability to transform an existing one.
tweets.summary_zh: 服务型企业总是受制于能提供结果的能力，员工的数量决定了它们的规模。以前无论需求多大，人才都是有限的，同时客户希望工作能更快、更便宜、质量更高。现在有了“智能助手”，这种情况发生了变化。一个工程师能做到以前需要好几个人的工作，一个设计师可以完成整个设计系统。他们的出现将大大提高效率，但同时仍然需要专家来确保结果正确。这意味着在网络安全、广告、法律、会计等很多只依赖人力的行业，我们将看到这种变化。如果你想创业或者转型这是个好时机。

Yes to all of this. As agents take on more and more long running project work, and you have swarms of agents that parallelize work against a goal, the agent harness and architecture for orchestration will have to evolve. 

One of the biggest shifts is how those agents collectively share their knowledge, keep track of the tasks, and also coordinate with human users. This in theory is technically straightforward, but there’s a ton of complexity to get right to ensure agents can both get access to the revenant resources without too much or little exposure.

There are a lot of lessons to pull from based on how people already do this kind of work together (people share their files, have computers to work with, community in chats and inboxes, and so on). But equally the primitives need to be able to enable this work at a throughput far higher than people, and in a world where agents can much more easily become a vector of security risk. 

Going to be super fun building out this next generation of how agents operate. Lots of opportunity here both for horizontal and vertical specific approaches to bring this to life.
tweets.summary_zh: 越来越多的智能系统（代理）需要协作来完成长时间的项目，这就要求我们改进如何管理和组织这些系统的方式。其中一个主要变化是这些代理如何分享知识、跟踪任务，并与人类用户协调。尽管技术上看起来简单，但实际上面临很多复杂性，比如确保代理可以有效获取所需资源而不带来安全风险。未来的工作会很有趣，充满了机会来探索更高效的解决方案。

tweets.text:
This post nails why we why we should take the Riemann Hypothesis breakthrough very seriously, even beyond math. We’re entering an era where solving problems will look very different from how we solved them in the past.

“This is not theory-building in the usual sense. It is something much weirder and more alien. The best human mathematicians know how to build theory, painstakingly, to reach a goal. But no human brain, on its own, is capable of creating a wormhole that requires a 25,000 page long tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious or realistic connection to the goal. But huge credit to Levent here: I think no current AI, on its own, is capable of this either.”

It used to be the case that to solve a particular problem - code, life sciences, math, cyber, engineering, and so on - you were ultimately bound by how much information an individual or team could retain and understand about the space. More information or more team members don’t always help, because it gets harder to connect the dots or coordinate amongst everyone. AI changes that completely. 

For the first time ever we can decouple the human context limits and ability to work through information from our ability to drive productivity or discoveries. This is likely not just a small increase in the kinds of discoveries we can drive, but a qualitative shift in human output. 

Now every single form of prior art, insight, past research, past decision, or unrelated breakthrough, can be used for the discovery or creation of something new. This is useful for anything from cybersecurity to life sciences research. Agents will be able to correlate entirely unrelated work to a separate project; scan every bit of data in your enterprise for solving a problem; and so on. 

The solutions may not be as elegant as they were in the past, but we sure will have far more of them. We’re only in the first couple of months of actually understanding the implications of this but it’s clearly going to drive a lot of change.
tweets.summary_zh: 最近的一个数学突破可能会改变我们解决问题的方式，不仅仅是数学领域。以前，解决问题主要依赖于人类的理解和团队的合作，但现在有了人工智能（AI），我们可以把这些限制打破，让机器帮助我们找到更多、更复杂的解决方案。虽然这些解决方案可能不如以前优雅，但数量会大大增加，对各个领域都非常有帮助，比如网络安全和生命科学研究。总之，未来的发现和创造将会与以往大不相同。

tweets.text:
This year we’ve had a clear jump in model capability where instead of telling agents precisely what to do, it’s better to use these systems to solve problems you can’t easily define yourself. 

A year ago you’d need to very clearly tell agents the how to design and develop your product idea, or there was almost no chance of success. Now, increasingly, the agent likely can come up with a better implementation than you’d have thought of because you can have it connect the dots between a far greater solution space than you can. 

This will be increasingly true in basically every domain of kneeler work. We’re going to see this impact in finance, legal, life sciences, cyber, and many other spaces where no person can hold onto all the available relevant industry knowledge to think of the best solution. 

Ultimately this is going to reshape our relationship with AI and how we deploy agents in our work. It won’t be about explicitly telling them, but instead giving them goals and enough freedom to pursue them in the best way they can.
tweets.summary_zh: 今年，AI模型的能力有了很大提升，我们不用再详细指示它们该怎么做，而是让它们帮助解决那些我们自己难以明确的问题。以前我们必须清晰地告诉AI怎么设计和开发产品，但现在AI能提出比我们更好的解决方案，因为它可以整合的信息比我们想象的要多得多。这个趋势将在金融、法律、生命科学等多个领域大显身手，改变我们与AI的关系，未来我们只需给它们设定目标，让它们自由去探索最佳解决方案。

tweets.text:
As these network attacks and impersonation attempts happen, who's securing the elderly? 

Especially thinking about my parents and grandparents.

There are four layers I can think through where this could work.

One is at the browser level, where somebody builds a secure browser that ensures that whatever websites they're going to are secured. Texts typically lead to a link, even for payments. This is why browser is key.

Two could be at the network layer, where there is a physical device, similar to Pi-hole, or an Onavo-like VPN on your phone, that blocks websites that could be deemed unsafe.

Three could be at the payments layer, where transactions that look like scams get flagged before the money leaves.

And fourth and most crazy could be at the phone level, where everything is monitored, and you're only getting calls from your loved ones. Cloned voices would work with a provider like Reality Defender. 

There are individual solutions for this today but none neatly packaged. 

This could all be packaged with insurance that covers any activities on the OS or phone. In that way, incentives are aligned to keep this on the edge.

The buyer would be the kids, someone like me, who get alerted when something looks off.

Regardless of what it’s called, we’re clearly moving to yet another era of AI agents in our work. 

We’ve quickly jumped from agents that spit out a quick answer for you, to today agents that you orchestrate inside of a set of tasks. But as agents can both fan out and work in parallel, handle much larger context, be able to do long running work, and have far greater levels of capabilities, we’re entering yet another level of what we can have AI do for us.

We’ll soon be able to give agents a set of goals, and they can go out and design the best solution for that goal, while also continuously improving it based on the ongoing execution of whatever it built. This will obviously start with engineering because that’s where we’re seeing the best practices emerge first in almost every new era of agents. 

But the impact can be quite massive across the rest of knowledge work. You’ll tell an agent to improve your client onboarding workflow to achieve a certain targeted goal; or have agents go reduce risk in your business; or improve your security posture on an ongoing basis.

These autonomous systems will be able to take on a set of goals, design the best outcome, test and iterate, deploy, and then optimize whatever it built on an ongoing basis. Importantly, this leads to outcomes and results that humans literally couldn’t have accomplished before. This will lead to fairly new levels of productivity with AI.

tweets.text:
My top 5 takeaways from @nateparrott on how to get Claude to design without AI slop:

1. Give Claude context upfront.

Share screenshots, pages you like, and your past work. For an existing product, have Claude rebuild the real screens from code.

2. Research familiar UX patterns.

For hard layout problems, ask Claude to research familiar products that solve something similar and note the layouts people already know how to use.

3. Make Claude aware of its design biases.

"The model has no idea what its own biases are." In your design.md or another file, consider discouraging Claude's tells like serif text, off-white backgrounds, and card-edge bars.

4. Start with wireframes.

Have Claude create wireframes first and give it feedback to nail your core user flows before going deep on fonts and colors.

5. Ask for multiple options, then remix them.

Ask Claude for 5 options for key screens with different fonts, colors, and styles. Then pick the parts you like and ask it to remix and create 5 more options.

📌 Watch the full episode now: https://t.co/HPX5HjXafX

Also available as a written post: https://t.co/jcofmkQc01
tweets.summary_zh:
从 @nateparrott 那里学到的如何让 Claude（一个 AI 设计助手）设计得更好的五个要点：

1. 提前给 Claude 足够的背景信息，比如喜欢的页面、截图和自己过去的作品。
2. 让 Claude 研究一些大家熟悉的用户体验（UX）设计模式，特别是在复杂布局上。
3. 让 Claude 知道它自己的设计偏见，比如避免使用衬线字体（有装饰的字体）和特定的背景颜色。
4. 先让 Claude 画出线框图（基础设计图），并针对用户体验给予反馈，确认重要的使用流程。
5. 要求 Claude 提供多个设计选项，然后挑选喜欢的部分再让它进行改进。

完整内容可以去链接观看或阅读，觉得学到的挺实用的！

tweets.text:
The chart of token spend per employee still has no ceiling in sight. And the closer you are to AI right now the deeper the sense is that we’re actually still in the early part of the curve of token use and adoption. 

This summer and fall’s model releases have continued to push the state of the art forward at a rate that already felt hard to maintain. As a result, for most productive use-cases the models are only now starting to actually work, and the feeling is that things will only accelerate from here.

Coding, in retrospect, was basically trash even 12 months ago. Now it’s finally starting to get good. And now that coding is actually working, you’re getting tool and computer use, which open up a wide variety of knowledge work domains that weren’t possible to throw agents at before.

Once you have agents that can code, use computers, leverage any tool out there, and understand a variety of domains, you can begin to throw them at a wide variety of knowledge work tasks that were hard to bring automation to across finance, life sciences, cyber, and more. So that brings agents to a broad set of work that we’re not really using them in yet at scale. 

Then comes the new form factors of agents. Agent swarms and background agents are going to eat up vastly more tokens than anything we can imagine. You’ll have agents running in most enterprises workflows processing data, validating work, doing research, providing decision support, and so on. And we’ll have swarms that fan out in parallel in areas like cyber, life sciences, coding, and more.

So basically tokens are only going up from here.
